extracted.intended_audience: educators, college trustees, and advocates/critics of scientific education (late-19th-century educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and principles for founding, organizing, and judging a college or curriculum emphasizing physical science, and broader standards for what constitutes 'culture' and appropriate social/organizational design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of party politics in college work
rubrics_metrics.description: "Party politics are forbidden to enter into the minds of either, so far as the work of the college is concerned."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit injunction by the founder: administrators and teachers must keep party politics out of the college's educational work. Intended as a governance constraint to preserve educational mission and impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of theology from college precincts
rubrics_metrics.description: "Theology is as sternly banished from its precincts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Founder-prescribed restriction: theological instruction or theological influences are to be excluded from the college. Presented as a condition for focusing on secular scientific instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: No provision for 'mere literary instruction and education'
rubrics_metrics.description: The trust "especially declared that the college shall make no provision for 'mere literary instruction and education.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A curricular constraint: the college should not devote itself to traditional classical/literary courses (as understood by the founder) but instead prioritize practical/scientific instruction. Huxley discusses and defends this prohibition against critics who equate 'culture' with classical literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough scientific education as essential to industrial progress
rubrics_metrics.description: "The diffusion of thorough scientific education is an absolutely essential condition of industrial progress."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justificatory standard for prioritizing scientific curricula: colleges serving industrial districts should provide rigorous scientific instruction because it directly advances practical industry and livelihoods. Used to evaluate whether an institution's mission aligns with regional economic needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustees should have large freedom to adjust arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir Josiah Mason "has left very large freedom of action to the trustees ... so that they may be able to adjust its arrangements in accordance with the changing conditions of the future."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governance principle: institutional charters should grant trustees flexibility to adapt curriculum and organization over time to meet changing needs. Presented as a design recommendation for institutional longevity and responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid organization in excess of need
rubrics_metrics.description: "Organization in excess of need prevents the attainment of that larger size and accompanying higher organization which might else have arisen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational design principle: build only the level of organization necessary for current orderly operation; over-elaboration creates inertia and impedes future growth and readjustment. Anti-pattern: completing organization beyond immediate need leads to rigidity and arrested growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh costs of maintaining political organization against benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: "Maintenance of it is costly; and the cost may become a greater evil than the evils escaped. It necessarily imposes restraints; and these restraints may become so extreme that anarchy, with all its miseries, is preferable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation criterion for political/administrative organization: consider the maintenance costs and restraints imposed; if disadvantages outweigh benefits, the organization is poorly designed. Use cost-benefit reasoning when judging institutional structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization creates resistance to reorganization
rubrics_metrics.description: "Organization as it becomes established is an obstacle to reorganization. Both by the inertia of position, and by the cohesion gradually established among them, the units of the structures formed oppose change."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive principle: established structures develop inertia and vested cohesion that resist change. When assessing institutions, account for internal resistance as a barrier to reform and plan for mechanisms to overcome it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession by inheritance favors stability; succession by efficiency favors change
rubrics_metrics.description: "Succession by inheritance is thus the principle of social rigidity; while succession by efficiency is the principle of social plasticity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy criterion for personnel/office succession: choosing successors by descent preserves stability and resists innovation; choosing them by demonstrated fitness promotes adaptability and reform. Use this to evaluate recruitment or succession rules' likely systemic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fill vacancies according to fitness to promote change
rubrics_metrics.description: "Stability is favored if the vacancies they leave are filled without dispute by descendants; while change is favored if the vacancies are filled by those who are experimentally proved to be best fitted for them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance on appointments: prefer merit/experimental proof of fitness where the goal is organizational adaptation and improvement; prefer hereditary filling where continuity and stability are the priorities. Huxley frames this as a trade-off between rigidity and plasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture defined as criticism of life requiring an ideal and theoretic standard
rubrics_metrics.description: "Culture ... implies the possession of an ideal, and the habit of critically estimating the value of things by comparison with a theoretic standard. Perfect culture should supply a complete theory of life, based upon a clear knowledge alike of its possibilities and of its limitations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational outcome criterion: an education that aspires to produce 'culture' must teach students to form ideals and apply critical/theoretical evaluation to life. Use this as a metric for curricular success beyond mere technical skill or learning facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature alone is insufficient to supply the criticism of life (culture)
rubrics_metrics.description: "... it is not self-evident that we have laid a sufficiently broad and deep foundation for that criticism of life which constitutes culture" by literature alone; "literature alone is not competent to supply this knowledge."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricular scope criterion: to achieve true 'culture' curricula must include physical science and other branches beyond classical literature, because scientific conceptions of the universe materially inform a criticism of life. Anti-pattern: equating 'culture' solely with classical literary training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method: appeal to nature and evidence; avoid assertions beyond evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "This scientific 'criticism of life' ... appeals not to authority, nor to what anybody may have thought or said, but to nature. ... It warns us that the assertion which outstrips evidence is not only a blunder but a crime."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epistemic standard for inquiry and teaching: prioritize evidence-based reasoning and empirical appeal over appeals to authority or sentiment. Educational programs should inculcate humility about claims and insist on evidence. Use as an evaluative criterion for disciplinary rigor and intellectual honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between non-coercive and coercive forms of organization
rubrics_metrics.description: "The organization which cooperation implies is of two kinds, distinct in origin and nature. The one, arising directly from the pursuit of individual ends ... develops unconsciously and is non-coercive. The other, arising directly from the pursuit of social ends ... develops consciously and is coercive."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic criterion for organizational design: identify whether structures arise voluntarily from individuals' pursuits or are consciously created to enforce social ends; the two have different origins, dynamics, and implications for freedom and coercion. Use this distinction when evaluating governance structures or policy instruments.
